tldr: AI INDUSTRY - Nvidia told server makers to stop shipping AI systems to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia after new US export rules.
INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS - Baghdad moved to take over Kurdistan's border crossings and northern oilfields with court backing; thousands protested in Erbil.
ECONOMICS - US third-quarter growth was revised up to a 4.3% annual rate from 3.4%; Trump called the first number fake and demanded an investigation.
HEALTHCARE - Bristol Myers Squibb's pill Sotyktu worked in one of two large lupus trials and missed in the other.
WILDCARD / AI INDUSTRY - The Bank of England put the biggest AI companies' potential exposure above $4 trillion and called the financing "complex, circular and opaque."
WILDCARD / AI INDUSTRY - Switzerland's cyber agency said AI agents ran five attacks, four of them successful, three aimed at power, water and telecom operators.
WILDCARD / INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS - Two Italian defence technicians were killed by a drone strike on a Kuwaiti air-defence site; Italy blames Iran, which denies it.
WILDCARD / ECONOMICS - EU leaders put forward Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos as the next European Central Bank president.
TECH - Ukraine said a 4-kilowatt laser shot down a Russian jet-powered drone, which would be a first.
TRUMP NEWS - A judge blocked the FCC's early review of ABC's licences, writing that its chairman "has taken President Trump's rhetoric as his marching orders."

items.headline: Nvidia tells server partners to stop AI shipments to four Southeast Asian countries
items.body: Nvidia has instructed server-making partners, including Dell and Supermicro, to stop delivering AI systems to customers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, according to the Financial Times, the Wall Street Journal and Nikkei Asia. The pause follows a mid-November Commerce Department rule requiring a licence to export or re-export advanced AI chips to those four countries and Brazil, aimed at Chinese companies renting computing power abroad. The WSJ reported the halt runs for an unspecified period while Nvidia assesses whether partners meet the requirements. Nvidia has not confirmed the instruction, and shares in Southeast Asian data-centre suppliers fell.
items.plain: Nvidia makes the chips nearly all serious AI work runs on, and other firms bolt them into the room-sized computers that fill data centres. Washington's worry is not those four countries but that a Chinese company barred from buying chips can rent time on a machine in Singapore instead. A licence is now required, so Nvidia stopped shipping rather than guess who the end customer is. Nvidia has said nothing publicly; this comes from reporters' sources.
items.why: Enforcement has shifted from border officials to Nvidia's own order book, which makes the company the gatekeeper deciding which countries get to build an AI industry.

items.headline: Baghdad takes over Kurdistan's borders and northern oilfields as thousands protest in Erbil
items.body: Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered federal authorities on 24 November to take control of every border crossing in the Kurdistan region and of oilfields in Kirkuk, Nineveh, Salahuddin and Diyala held by Kurdish forces, after a smuggling investigation at the state-run North Oil Company. Iraq's Federal Supreme Court affirmed federal authority over borders, oil operations and public revenues on 25 November, with two judges dissenting. Thousands rallied at the Erbil citadel on Thursday, and the Kurdistan Regional Government said it rejected "any attempt to return Iraq to a centralised system." Two crossings with Iran and Syria have closed, and Baghdad denied reports of troop movements toward the region.
items.plain: Iraqi Kurdistan is a northern region that runs much of its own affairs, including its border posts and, until this week, its own oil arrangements. Oil pays for about 90% of Iraq's budget, so controlling the wells and the crossings is really about controlling the money. Baghdad says Kurdish officials allowed smuggling; Erbil says Baghdad never paid what it owed. The court ruling matters because it turns a political move into a legal one, which is harder to undo.
items.why: Kurdish autonomy has rested on controlling its own oil and borders, and losing both by court order removes the leverage the region has used since 2005 without a shot being fired.

sources.outlet: Associated Press via The Washington Times

items.headline: US third-quarter growth revised up to 4.3%, and Trump demands an investigation into the first estimate
items.body: The Bureau of Economic Analysis raised its estimate of third-quarter US growth to a 4.3% annual rate on 25 November, up from the 3.4% it first reported, citing stronger business investment and revised consumer spending. Measured over the three months rather than annualised, that is about 1.1%. Trump responded in a Thanksgiving post calling the original figure "FAKE," describing the gap as "a massive, and purposeful, error" and demanding an immediate investigation into why the correct number was not released before the election. He offered no evidence. Revisions this size are routine; the BEA revised second-quarter 2020 growth by more. The next estimate is due 23 December.
items.plain: The BEA is the federal office that measures how fast the economy grew. It publishes an early estimate, then corrects it twice as late tax, trade and company data arrive, which is why the number moves. This revision moved growth up, not down, which is the part that does not fit the complaint. The agency sits inside the Commerce Department, run by Trump's own appointee, who fired the head of the labour statistics bureau last year over different revisions.
items.why: Investors, the Federal Reserve and every forecaster price off these releases, so pressure on the agencies that produce them raises the cost of borrowing long before it changes a single number.

items.headline: Bristol Myers Squibb's Sotyktu succeeds in one lupus trial and fails the other
items.body: Bristol Myers Squibb reported on 25 November that Sotyktu (deucravacitinib), a pill already approved for psoriasis, met its main goal in one of two Phase 3 trials in systemic lupus erythematosus and missed in the other. In POETYK SLE-1, with 510 adults, significantly more patients on Sotyktu reached an SRI-4 response at week 52 than on placebo, with significant results on secondary measures including steroid tapering and fatigue. POETYK SLE-2, with 513 adults, missed its primary endpoint; the company said the drug's response matched SLE-1 but the placebo response was higher. Safety matched the drug's known profile. BMS will review the full dataset with regulators.
items.plain: Lupus is a disease in which the immune system attacks the body's own tissue, and most patients are managed with steroids that cause harm of their own over time. A daily pill that let people cut their steroid dose would matter, so this drug was tested in two near-identical trials. One worked and one did not, for a specific reason: patients given the dummy pill improved more than expected, which shrinks the measurable gap even if the drug performed the same.
items.why: A split result on 1,023 patients leaves the FDA to judge whether an unusually strong placebo response excuses a missed trial, a question that has sunk lupus drugs before.

sources.outlet: The American Journal of Managed Care

items.headline: Bank of England puts the biggest AI companies' exposure above $4 trillion
items.body: The Bank of England's Financial Stability Report, published Thursday, put the potential AI exposure of the largest cloud and AI companies at just over $4 trillion, a figure built from debt plus off-balance-sheet items including leases, purchase commitments and contingent obligations. The Financial Policy Committee called AI financing "increasingly complex, circular and opaque" and said equity valuations remain "stretched" and dependent on those companies delivering the profits investors expect. The report projects hyperscaler bond issuance above $305 billion in 2026, around 8% of global investment-grade issuance. The same committee proposed cutting capital requirements for major UK lenders by a further 30 basis points.
items.plain: Hyperscalers are the few companies that own most of the world's cloud computing, and they now borrow on a scale that ranks them among the largest corporate bond issuers anywhere. The $4 trillion is not money lost or even all borrowed; it adds the long leases and purchase promises that never appear as debt. "Circular" is the key word: a chip maker invests in an AI firm, which spends it on that maker's chips, and the same dollar counts twice.
items.why: A central bank has now attached an official number and the word "opaque" to AI credit, which is what regulators do shortly before they start asking banks to hold capital against it.

items.headline: Swiss cyber agency says AI agents carried out five attacks, four of them successful
items.body: Switzerland's Federal Office for Cybersecurity said on Thursday that AI agents were used in five recent cyberattacks in the country and that four of them succeeded, Reuters reported. Three of the five targeted critical-infrastructure operators, which the Swiss broadcaster SRF identified as electricity, water and telecommunications providers. Cyber chief Florian Schütz said there were no major outages. The agency did not name the operators, identify who was behind the attacks, describe the tools used, or quantify losses. It told operators to patch internet-facing vulnerabilities within 24 hours. Italy's national cyber response team has flagged similar autonomous campaigns.
items.plain: An AI agent is a model given a goal and the ability to act on its own, running commands and reacting to what it finds instead of waiting for a human at each step. Applied to hacking, that removes the slow and expensive part: a skilled person probing a network by hand. The telling detail is the ratio, four of five attempts got in. Switzerland has not said who did it, so the attribution is genuinely unknown.
items.why: It is the first time a national government has attributed successful breaches of power, water and telecom operators to AI agents, which turns a widely predicted threat into a documented one.

items.headline: Two Italian defence technicians killed in drone strike on Kuwaiti air-defence site
items.body: Two Italian technicians working for Rheinmetall Italia were killed on Thursday while servicing air-defence detection antennas at a Kuwaiti military surveillance station, Italy's foreign ministry said. Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani told the Senate in Rome that Iranian drones had targeted the site. Kuwait's defence ministry first reported four people wounded by falling debris before saying the two men had died. A spokesman for Iran's armed forces denied any Iranian operation in the region and called it a "false flag"; Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi repeated the denial to Tajani by phone. Italy will lodge a complaint with Iran's embassy, and the EU called for more pressure on Tehran.
items.plain: Kuwait sits across the top of the Persian Gulf from Iran and hosts Western military equipment, so it has been struck repeatedly during this year's fighting between the United States and Iran. The men killed were not soldiers but contractors from an Italian arms firm, repairing the radar that spots incoming drones. That is what makes this larger than a casualty count: the dead are citizens of a NATO member, and Iran flatly denies firing.
items.why: European governments have kept their distance from the US campaign against Iran, and two dead Italians working on NATO-supplied equipment make that distance harder to hold.

items.headline: EU leaders name Spain's Hernández de Cos as the next ECB president
items.body: The European Council on Thursday put forward Pablo Hernández de Cos as the next president of the European Central Bank. He was governor of the Bank of Spain from 2018 to 2024 and is now general manager of the Bank for International Settlements, and would be the first Spaniard and the fifth person to hold the post since 1998. France and Germany agreed on him as their joint candidate, alongside two other executive board appointments: Laurence Boone of France and Markus Brunnermeier of Germany. The Council must still consult the European Parliament and the ECB's governing council. Christine Lagarde said on 30 October that she will leave on 7 February 2027.
items.plain: The ECB sets interest rates for the 20 countries that use the euro, so one committee in Frankfurt decides what a mortgage costs from Lisbon to Helsinki. The Bank for International Settlements, where the nominee works now, is effectively the central bank for central banks. The steps still to come are consultations, not contests: the real decision was France and Germany agreeing on one name. Analysts read him as a continuity pick rather than a change of direction.
items.why: Lagarde's early exit means the eurozone's rate-setting for the next eight years was settled in a Franco-German bargain months before anyone expected the seat to open.

items.headline: Ukraine says a laser downed a Russian jet-powered drone for the first time
items.body: Ukraine said a laser weapon shot down a Russian jet-powered Geran attack drone, which would be the first such interception. Presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov announced it on 25 November and posted a 21-second video of the engagement, saying the system was guarding a critical-infrastructure site. The weapon, called Blysk and built by the private firm Carmine Sky, is a roughly 4-kilowatt test unit that disables drones by overheating their internal components. Beskrestnov said it is "still too early to discuss serial production." The footage does not identify the drone type and no independent confirmation has been published.
items.plain: Shooting down a cheap drone with a missile costs far more than the drone did, which is the arithmetic that makes these attacks worth repeating. A laser inverts it: expensive once, then each shot costs only electricity. The catch is power. At four kilowatts, about what a kitchen oven draws, the beam cannot blow a drone apart; it has to hold one spot long enough to cook the electronics, which is hard at jet speed and impossible through cloud.
items.why: Even an unconfirmed kill at four kilowatts matters because the cost per shot, not the kill itself, is what decides whether a defender can outlast a drone campaign.

items.headline: Judge blocks FCC review of ABC licences, finding the agency took Trump's posts as instructions
items.body: Judge Loren AliKhan of the US District Court for the District of Columbia granted ABC a preliminary injunction on 25 November barring the FCC from proceeding with early renewal reviews of the network's eight broadcast licences, and denied the agency's motion to dismiss. In a 45-page opinion she found ABC likely to succeed on its claim that the FCC retaliated against speech that offended Trump and FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, writing "This is not a close case" and "Chairman Carr has taken President Trump's rhetoric as his marching orders." She noted the commission opened the early review in April, one day after Trump posted that Jimmy Kimmel should be fired. The FCC called the decision "wrong on the facts and wrong on the law." It is a preliminary ruling, not a final judgment, and the agency must report on its compliance by 2 December.
items.plain: Television stations need a federal licence to broadcast, renewed on a schedule, and the FCC decides. Calling eight of ABC's licences in for early review puts the network's permission to operate on the table without denying anything. The judge's finding is about timing and motive: the review opened the day after the president publicly demanded a late-night host be fired. A preliminary injunction means she thinks ABC will probably win, not that the case is over.
items.why: A federal judge has put in the record that the FCC's chairman treated presidential posts as instructions, which is the finding that makes every future licence action against a broadcaster reviewable for retaliation.
